14960:
Trickery means the deliberate use of clever, dishonest acts or schemes to make someone believe something that is not true, or to gain an unfair advantage over them.

The key word here is deliberate. Trickery is never an accident. The person using trickery knows exactly what they are doing and has chosen to be dishonest. They are crafting a plan — sometimes simple, sometimes elaborate — to mislead or manipulate someone else.

Think of it this way: if lying is a single dishonest statement, trickery is the whole game being played around it.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

Trickery almost always carries a negative meaning. When you use this word, you are saying that something unfair and dishonest is happening. It implies cleverness — but cleverness being used for selfish or harmful purposes. You could think of trickery as "smart dishonesty."

There is one exception: in entertainment contexts, like magic shows, the word can be used in a lighter, almost admiring way — because the audience willingly agrees to be fooled. Even then, the word keeps a slightly playful edge. Outside of entertainment, trickery is nearly always a criticism.

Trickery is not a one-size word — it covers a wide range of situations.

On the lighter end, a child who hides a vegetable under their mashed potato so it looks like they've eaten it is using trickery. Harmless, but still dishonest and intentional.

In the middle range, a car salesman who deliberately hides known defects in a vehicle to close a sale is using trickery to gain an unfair financial advantage.

On the serious end, a con artist who creates a fake investment company, forges documents, and builds an elaborate false identity to steal people's life savings is using trickery in its most dangerous and harmful form.

The word comfortably fits all of these situations. Context tells you where on the scale the trickery falls.

Trickery is not simply making a mistake. If someone gives you wrong information because they genuinely believed it was true, that is an error, not trickery.

Trickery is also not just a single lie. It suggests a method — a pattern of dishonest behavior, or a crafted scheme. A person who uses trickery has put thought into their deception.

Trickery is also not always obvious or dramatic. Some of the most effective trickery is quiet, subtle, and designed to go completely unnoticed.

"She obtained his signature through trickery, not consent."

"The villain relied on trickery because he lacked the strength to win fairly."

"He saw through their trickery immediately and refused to hand over the money."

"The magician's performance was all trickery, and the crowd was delighted by it."

"The company rose to power through trickery and deceit, not honest competition."

Through trickery — used to describe how something was obtained or achieved by dishonest means. ("She got the job through trickery.")

Resort to trickery — to decide to use deceptive methods, often when honest approaches have failed or when someone lacks the ability to succeed fairly. ("When persuasion failed, he resorted to trickery.")

Sheer trickery — emphasizes that something was achieved purely by dishonest means, with zero genuine merit. ("His win was sheer trickery.")

Trick (noun/verb) — a single dishonest or clever act. Trickery is the broader practice of using such acts.

Tricky (adjective) — something that is cleverly difficult or deceptive in nature. Also used informally to describe something that is just genuinely difficult.

Trickster (noun) — a person who habitually uses tricks and deception to get what they want.
How Trickery Differs From Similar Words

Deception is the broad, umbrella term for any act of making someone believe something false. Trickery is a type of deception — one that implies cleverness and a crafted method. All trickery is deception, but not all deception is trickery.

Fraud is a legal term for serious, criminal deception — usually involving money. Trickery is informal and much broader; you can use it to describe everything from a child's prank to a criminal scam.

Manipulation usually refers to controlling someone's feelings or thinking to get them to do what you want. Trickery is more about crafted acts or clever schemes designed to fool someone.

Cunning describes the quality of being cleverly dishonest — it's an adjective describing a person's character. Trickery describes the actual acts or practices themselves.

Trickery is the intentional use of clever, dishonest acts or schemes to fool someone, make them believe something false, or gain an unfair advantage — and it is almost universally considered to be morally wrong.
14961: To trickle means to flow slowly, gently, and in a very small, thin stream. Think of a tiny, quiet thread of water moving across a surface — not rushing, not pouring, just barely moving along in a thin line. That image is the heart of this word.

This word works on two levels — a literal one and a figurative one. Both are equally important and widely used.

1. Literal — for liquids

When a liquid trickles, it moves in a slow, thin, and small stream. The key qualities here are:

  • Small in amount — not a flood, not even a proper flow. Just a thin line of liquid.
  • Slow in speed — no rushing. It barely seems to be moving.
  • Continuous — it keeps going, drop by drop or in a thin thread, rather than all at once.

Examples:

  • Water trickled down the wall after the rain.
  • Tears trickled down her cheeks.
  • Blood trickled from the small cut on his finger.
  • Sweat trickled down his back in the summer heat.

Notice that in all these cases, there's nothing dramatic or forceful. The liquid is just quietly making its way, little by little.

2. Figurative — for people, information, money, or things

This is where the word becomes even more powerful and useful. When people, news, money, goods, or almost anything arrives or moves somewhere slowly, in small numbers or amounts, and gradually over time, we say it trickles.

You are essentially borrowing the image of a thin, slow stream of water and applying it to non-liquid things.

Examples:

  • Fans trickled into the stadium before the match. (They didn't all arrive at once — they came in slowly, a few at a time.)
  • News of the disaster slowly trickled out. (The information came out little by little, not all at once.)
  • Money trickled into his account over the months. (Small amounts came in gradually.)
  • Complaints began to trickle in after the product launched. (They came in slowly at first, not in a flood.)
  • Refugees trickled across the border. (A small, steady stream of people, not a crowd rushing through.)

The figurative use always carries that same feeling: slow, small, and gradual — never sudden, large, or all at once.

One of the most important things about this word is the mood and feeling it creates. It is almost always a quiet, gentle word. It suggests:

  • Lack of force or urgency — nothing is being pushed or rushed.
  • Small scale — whatever is moving is not doing so in large quantities.
  • Patience or slowness — things are happening, but barely, and over time.

This is why writers use it so often. It paints a picture very efficiently. Compare:

  • People walked into the hall. — Plain, tells you nothing about speed or number.
  • People trickled into the hall. — Immediately you picture a slow, sparse, quiet arrival.

The word does a lot of work in a small space.

You will very often see "trickle" paired with direction words. These are natural and common:

  • Trickle in / trickle into — to arrive slowly, in small amounts.

"Orders trickled in throughout the week."

  • Trickle out / trickle out of — to leave, leak, or be revealed slowly.

"Details of the scandal slowly trickled out to the press."

  • Trickle down — to move downward slowly (literally or figuratively).

"Water trickled down the rocks."
"Wealth trickled down to workers over time." (This is also used in economics to describe the idea that benefits to the rich gradually reach lower income groups — you may hear the phrase trickle-down economics.)

  • Trickle away — to slowly disappear, drain, or reduce over time.

"His savings trickled away over the years."
"Her energy trickled away as the illness continued."

Understanding a word also means knowing what it doesn't mean. Here's how trickle differs from similar words:

  • Drip — a single drop falling, or the action of drops falling one at a time. A drip is more about individual drops; a trickle is a thin, continuous thread.
  • Flow — movement of liquid in a larger, more steady volume. A river flows; a small crack in a wall trickles.
  • Pour — a large, fast, heavy release of liquid. The complete opposite of trickle in scale and force.
  • Gush — a sudden, fast burst of liquid in a large amount. Again, the opposite of trickle.
  • Stream — a flowing movement, usually larger and faster than a trickle.

Think of it as a scale: Trickle → Drip/Seep → Stream → Flow → Pour → Gush. Trickle sits at the smallest, slowest, gentlest end.

IdeaWhat "trickle" means
With liquidTo move slowly in a thin, small, gentle stream
With people/thingsTo arrive or move somewhere slowly, in small numbers, over time
SpeedSlow
AmountSmall
MoodGentle, quiet, gradual

After reading all of this, whenever you see or hear the word trickle, ask yourself: Is something moving slowly, in small amounts, gently — like a thin thread of water? If yes, that's your word.
14962: A trident is a long spear with three sharp points at one end, instead of just one. Picture a regular spear — now imagine three pointed tips sitting side by side at the top, like three teeth of a fork. That is a trident. The three prongs are usually the same length, equally sharp, and all point in the same direction. The handle is long, like a staff, allowing it to be gripped firmly or even thrown. It is, at once, a weapon, a tool, and one of the most instantly recognized shapes in human history.
The most famous trident — Poseidon and Neptune

The trident is most powerfully linked to Poseidon, the ancient Greek god of the sea, and his Roman counterpart, Neptune. In myths, the trident was Poseidon's personal weapon and the symbol of his authority. He used it to stir up storms, split the earth open, and command the ocean. Just as a king holds a scepter to show he is in charge, Poseidon held a trident. If you have ever seen a statue or painting of Neptune, he is almost always shown as a muscular, bearded figure gripping a long trident. This is exactly why, even today, the trident feels deeply connected to the ocean, to raw natural power, and to the idea of a god or ruler being in control.

Beyond mythology, the trident has had very practical uses across different eras and cultures.

As a fishing tool, the trident was extremely effective. Fishermen would wade into shallow water and spear fish directly. The three prongs were a clever design — even if the fish shifted slightly at the last moment, one of the prongs would still catch it. A single-pointed spear would miss far more often. This use is ancient and was common in many parts of the world.

As a weapon in gladiator combat, the trident played a famous role in ancient Rome. A type of gladiator called the retiarius fought with a trident in one hand and a weighted net in the other. The strategy was to throw the net over the opponent to trap them, then strike with the trident. This style of fighting was well-known and widely watched in Roman arenas.

Over thousands of years, the trident grew beyond being just a physical object and became a loaded symbol recognized across the world.

Because of its association with Poseidon and Neptune, a trident commonly represents mastery over the sea or the forces of nature. It carries a sense of immense, almost unstoppable power.

In Hinduism, the trident is called the trishula and is the weapon and symbol of Shiva, one of the most important gods in the religion. Here it carries deep spiritual meaning — the three prongs represent three fundamental forces: creation, preservation, and destruction. It is widely used in Hindu art, temples, and rituals.

The island nation of Barbados features a trident on its national flag, symbolizing the sea and a break from its colonial past.

Today, the word "trident" is used for many things beyond ancient spears and sea gods. It is the name of nuclear-armed submarines used by the American and British navies — chosen because the word suggests devastating power. It is a popular brand of chewing gum. Sports teams and companies use it in their logos and names. In every case, the word is deliberately chosen to evoke strength, sharpness, and authority.

"The statue of Neptune towered over the fountain, his trident raised toward the sky." "The fisherman stood knee-deep in the river, gripping his trident and watching the water for movement." "On the nation's flag, a golden trident stood against a deep blue background." "In the myth, the god drove his trident into the ground and the earth shook."

A trident is a three-pronged spear — a real historical weapon and fishing tool — that became one of the world's most enduring symbols of power, most famously belonging to the sea god Poseidon, and still widely recognized and used as a symbol today.
14963: The word trifle has two completely separate meanings — one abstract and one very concrete. A good learner must know both.
Meaning 1: Something unimportant or of little value

This is the heart of the word. A trifle is anything — an object, a matter, a problem, a sum of money — that is so small or minor that it barely deserves attention. It is something not worth taking seriously.

Think of it this way: if a friend spills a tiny drop of water on a table, that is a trifle. It is nothing. It doesn't matter. But if they spill an entire bucket of water, that is no longer a trifle — that is a real problem.

Examples:

  • "Don't worry about that scratch on the car — it's a mere trifle."
  • "He wasted his whole afternoon arguing over trifles." (here, trifles = small, silly matters)
  • "She paid only a trifle for that old book at the market." (here, a trifle = a very small amount of money)

The key feeling this word carries is dismissiveness — the suggestion that something is so small, it is almost beneath notice.
A special phrase built from this meaning: "a trifle"

When you place the phrase "a trifle" directly before an adjective, it acts as a gentle way of saying "slightly" or "a little bit." This is one of the most elegant and common uses of this word.

Examples:

  • "The soup is a trifle too salty." (= just slightly too salty)
  • "He looked a trifle embarrassed when she walked in." (= a little bit embarrassed)
  • "The room was a trifle cold, but nothing unbearable." (= mildly cold)

Notice how this phrase softens the statement. Instead of saying "very cold" or "very embarrassed," using "a trifle" makes the quality sound minor and almost barely worth mentioning — which is perfectly consistent with the word's core meaning.

Completely separate from the abstract meaning, a trifle is also a well-known dessert popular in Britain and other parts of the English-speaking world. It is a cold, layered dessert, typically built in a large glass bowl so that all the layers are visible from the outside. The classic layers, from bottom to top, are:

  1. Sponge cake, usually soaked in sherry (an alcoholic drink) or fruit juice to make it soft and moist
  2. Fruit — often strawberries, raspberries, or peaches
  3. Custard — a thick, creamy, yellow sauce made from eggs, milk, and sugar
  4. Whipped cream on top

It is a dessert associated with celebrations, holidays, and family gatherings in British culture, especially Christmas. The visual beauty of seeing all those layers stacked in a glass bowl is part of its appeal.
How the two meanings are connected (conceptually)

You might wonder: why does the same word mean both "something unimportant" and "a dessert"? Historically, the dessert got its name because it was considered a light, playful dish — not a serious, heavy meal. It was a small, sweet, whimsical thing. So both meanings share the same spirit: something light, not to be taken too seriously.
The full picture at a glance

• If someone calls your concern "a trifle," they are gently (or dismissively) telling you it is nothing worth worrying about.
  • If someone says you seem "a trifle confused," they mean you seem just a little confused — nothing major.
  • If someone invites you to have "some trifle" after dinner at a British home, you are about to eat a delicious layered cream dessert.

Master these three uses and you have completely mastered this word.
14964:
To trifle means to treat something or someone as if they are less important or less serious than they actually are — to handle them carelessly, dismissively, or with a kind of playful disrespect that the situation simply does not deserve.

Trifling is about a mismatch — the subject demands seriousness, but you're being casual, flippant, or even manipulative about it.
The Two Main Ways It Is Used

1. To trifle with someone or something

This is by far the most common pattern. When you trifle with a person, you treat their feelings, time, or dignity as though they don't really matter. You play with them lightly, without genuine care or commitment.

Examples:

  • "He trifled with her emotions for months, never being honest about how he truly felt."
  • "Don't trifle with me — I need a real answer, not excuses."
  • "She felt trifled with when he cancelled their plans for the third time without a real reason."

In all these cases, one person is treating another's sincerity, trust, or feelings as something casual and disposable — and that is the offence.

You can also trifle with things, not just people — particularly serious matters like rules, risks, or important decisions:

  • "You should not trifle with your health."
  • "The general warned his officers not to trifle with the safety protocols."
  • "Trifling with the law will only bring you trouble."

Here, the idea is the same: you're treating something weighty as though it were light — and the word carries a strong warning that this is a dangerous or disrespectful mistake.

2. To trifle (without "with") — wasting time or acting frivolously

In a slightly older or more literary usage, "trifle" can also mean to spend time on unimportant things, to dawdle, or to waste time on silly, meaningless activities when you should be doing something more serious.

Examples:

  • "Stop trifling and come help with the work."
  • "He trifled away the entire afternoon and accomplished nothing."
  • "She accused him of trifling instead of addressing the real problem."

In these sentences, trifling is about frittering away energy, time, or attention on things that don't matter. Think of it as treating your own time (or someone else's) as though it has no value.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

This is important: trifle is not a neutral word. It almost always carries a tone of disapproval, warning, or hurt. When someone says "don't trifle with me," they are not just making an observation — they are expressing that they feel disrespected, or that they are warning you of real consequences.

The word implies that the person or thing being trifled with deserves more seriousness than they are being given. There is a moral edge to it.

Compare:

  • "He played with her feelings." — Descriptive, slightly informal.
  • "He trifled with her feelings." — More formal, more pointed. It judges his behaviour as wrong and careless.
A Very Common Phrase: "Not to be trifled with"

One of the most frequently used expressions built on this verb is:

"X is not to be trifled with."

This means: X is serious, powerful, or dangerous — do not underestimate or treat X carelessly.

Examples:

  • "The ocean is not to be trifled with — even experienced swimmers have drowned in those waters."
  • "She may seem gentle, but she is not to be trifled with when it comes to protecting her family."
  • "The virus was not to be trifled with — it spread faster than anyone expected."

This phrase is very common in writing and speech, and knowing it will help you recognise the word in many real-world contexts.
Register: When Is This Word Used?

"Trifle" as a verb is formal to semi-formal. You would see it more in:

  • Books, literature, and journalism
  • Serious or emphatic speech
  • Warnings and criticisms

You are less likely to hear it in very casual everyday conversation, where people might instead say "don't mess with me" or "stop playing around." But trifle carries more gravity and precision than those informal alternatives.
How to Distinguish Trifle from Similar Words

Similar WordHow It Differs from "Trifle"
  • "Play with" — Similar idea, but much more casual and less judgmental. "Playing with someone's feelings" is common in everyday speech. "Trifling with someone's feelings" feels more formal and more condemnatory.
  • "Toy with" — Very close in meaning. "Toying with someone" implies a cat-and-mouse kind of manipulation, often with the idea that the person doing it is enjoying the power they hold. "Trifling" is more about careless dismissiveness than deliberate manipulation, though there is overlap.
  • "Dabble" — Dabble means to try something casually without real commitment, but it is not disapproving in the same way. You can "dabble in painting" without anyone being harmed. Trifling almost always suggests someone or something is being wronged by the lack of seriousness.
  • "Waste time" — A plain, flat description. "Trifling" has elegance and weight that "wasting time" lacks.
A Quick Summary to Anchor It All

To trifle is to treat something serious as though it were unimportant — to be carelessly dismissive of a person's feelings, a serious matter, or your own responsibilities. It almost always carries disapproval. The most common pattern is "trifle with", and the most common set phrase is "not to be trifled with."

If you remember one thing: trifling = treating something serious with undeserved casualness or disrespect.
14965:
To trifle with something or someone means to treat it without the seriousness, care, or respect it deserves. You are handling something important as if it were unimportant — dismissively, carelessly, or playfully, when the situation actually calls for seriousness.

Think of it this way: imagine someone handed you a priceless, fragile antique vase, and you started tossing it in the air and catching it like a ball. That is the spirit of "trifling with" something. You are not giving it the weight it deserves.

To understand the idiom deeply, it helps to understand the word "trifle" on its own.

As a noun, a trifle means something small, unimportant, or of little value. For example, a small problem you barely notice might be called "a mere trifle." The word itself carries the idea of smallness and insignificance.

As a verb, to trifle means to act in a silly, light, or non-serious way — to mess around instead of being focused.

So when you trifle with something, you are taking something that deserves serious attention and treating it as though it were a small, insignificant trifle. You are shrinking its importance in your mind and in your actions.
The Two Main Ways This Idiom Is Used

1. Trifling with a Person's Feelings or Emotions

This is perhaps the most common use. When someone trifles with your feelings, they play with your emotions carelessly — they flirt with you without being sincere, make you believe they care when they don't, or treat your trust as a game.

"He told her he loved her, but he was just trifling with her feelings."

Here, the person is not serious about the relationship. They are treating her emotions as something to play with, not something fragile and precious that deserves honesty and care. This use carries a strong sense of betrayal and disrespect.

2. Trifling with Something Serious or Important

You can also trifle with an important matter — a rule, a law, a risk, a responsibility — by not taking it seriously enough.

"You should not trifle with your health by skipping the doctor's advice."

"The general warned his soldiers not to trifle with the enemy's strength."

In these cases, the idiom warns against underestimating or casually dismissing something that could have serious consequences.
The Most Famous Form: "Not to Be Trifled With"

You will very frequently hear this idiom in the negative warning form:

"She is not someone to be trifled with."

"This disease is not to be trifled with."

This phrasing is a strong warning. It means: "This person or thing is serious, powerful, or dangerous — do not treat them lightly or you will regret it."

When someone says "he is not to be trifled with," they are telling you that this person is formidable — they have power, authority, or will not tolerate being disrespected. Approach with full seriousness.
The Emotional Tone of This Idiom

"Trifle with" almost always carries a negative tone. It is used in situations involving:

  • Disapproval — "How dare you trifle with such a serious matter?"
  • Warning — "Do not trifle with forces you don't understand."
  • Hurt or indignation — "I will not allow anyone to trifle with my dignity."

It is rarely, if ever, used in a neutral or positive context.
The Register: When and Where Is This Idiom Used?

"Trifle with" is slightly formal and literary in tone. You are more likely to encounter it in:

  • Books, novels, and literature
  • Formal speeches or writing
  • Serious warnings in conversation

In casual everyday speech, people might instead say "play with," "mess with," or "toy with" — these are the informal cousins of "trifle with" and carry very similar meanings.
Side-by-Side Comparisons to Lock In the Meaning

Instead of saying...You could say...
"Don't play around with her emotions.""Don't trifle with her emotions."
"He's a dangerous man. Be careful.""He is not a man to be trifled with."
"She's not taking the deadline seriously.""She is trifling with the deadline."

Here is a simple way to remember this idiom forever:

A trifle = something tiny and unimportant.
To trifle with something = to make it seem tiny and unimportant — even when it isn't.

So whenever you "trifle with" something serious, you are insulting it with smallness.

"Trifle with" means to treat a serious person, feeling, or matter in a careless, playful, or disrespectful way — as if it doesn't deserve real attention. It warns that something or someone is being dangerously underestimated or disrespectfully handled. The phrase "not to be trifled with" is a strong caution that something is powerful and must be approached with full seriousness.
14966:
Something is trifling when it is so small, unimportant, or insignificant that it barely deserves to be noticed or taken seriously. If you call something trifling, you are saying it is too minor and too petty to merit real attention or real concern.

Think of it this way: imagine someone spills a single drop of water on the floor and immediately calls a cleaning crew to deal with it. You'd probably think, "That's such a trifling problem — why make a fuss about it?" The drop is so insignificant that the reaction is wildly out of proportion to it.
The Tone It Carries — This Is the Key

This is where "trifling" becomes interesting and unique. The word doesn't just describe something as small — it also carries a quiet tone of dismissal or mild contempt. When you call something trifling, you are subtly saying, "This is so beneath notice that it's almost embarrassing to even bring it up." There's a slight edge of impatience baked into the word.

For example, if your boss calls your concerns a "trifling matter," they are not simply saying the concerns are minor. They are dismissing you — suggesting you are wasting everyone's time by raising them. This is what separates "trifling" from a plain word like "small." Small is just a description. Trifling is a judgment.

To describe a matter, issue, or concern that is too minor to deserve serious attention: "They argued for hours over a trifling disagreement." The argument is so petty and small that the time and energy spent on it seem absurd.

To describe an amount — almost always of money — that is embarrassingly small, almost insulting in its smallness: "After five years of hard work, the company offered her a trifling pay raise of fifty cents an hour." The raise is so small it's almost an insult rather than a reward.

In both uses, the idea is identical: the thing in question is so minor that it almost doesn't count.

Trifling is never neutral. The moment you use it, you are making a judgment — you are saying the thing does not deserve respect or serious attention.

Also, "trifling" is not about physical size. You would not say "a trifling ant" or "a trifling pebble." It applies to the importance, value, or weight of something — not its physical dimensions. A trifling matter. A trifling sum. A trifling concern. A trifling objection.

"Trifling" sits in a slightly formal, literary register. It sounds more polished and deliberate than everyday alternatives. In casual speech, people tend to say things like "no big deal," "trivial," "minor," or "not worth it." But in written English — in books, formal essays, serious correspondence — "trifling" fits naturally and carries more rhetorical punch. It sounds intentional. When a writer chooses "trifling" over "minor," they are making a point, not just describing.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Knowing where "trifling" sits among its close relatives is one of the best ways to pin down exactly what it means.

Trivial is the closest synonym and can often be swapped with "trifling." However, "trivial" is more emotionally neutral — it simply means unimportant, without the extra sting of dismissal that "trifling" carries.

Petty is often used to describe a person being unnecessarily small-minded, whereas "trifling" describes the thing or matter itself as being small.

Negligible means something is so small it can safely be ignored. It is more clinical and detached — a word used in scientific or mathematical contexts ("a negligible difference in temperature"), without any emotional charge.

Paltry is very close to "trifling," especially when describing an amount of money. A paltry sum and a trifling sum mean nearly the same thing — embarrassingly small. The difference is that "paltry" is used almost exclusively for amounts, while "trifling" is broader and applies to matters, concerns, and objections too.

Insignificant is the most plain and neutral of the group — it means not significant, with no particular emotional flavor attached.

The unique value of "trifling" is that it combines the meaning of "small and unimportant" with a tone of dismissal or mild contempt. None of the other words do both things as clearly and elegantly in a single word.

Here are several examples that show the word in action. Read each one and notice how it tells you the thing is small AND implies it is not worth your energy:

"The king waved away the messenger's concerns as trifling distractions." — The king is saying the concerns are too minor for someone of his importance to bother with.

"She was insulted by the trifling amount they offered for her painting." — The offer was so low it was almost offensive.

"Don't let trifling setbacks discourage you from your goals." — The setbacks are small and not worth letting slow you down.

"He spent his days on trifling arguments instead of tackling real problems." — The arguments were so petty they weren't worth the energy they consumed.

"A trifling error in the report was quietly corrected before it was sent." — A tiny, barely noticeable mistake.
A Simple Test for Using It Correctly

Before using "trifling," ask yourself two things: Is this thing so minor that a reasonable person would consider it barely worth mentioning? And do you want to suggest that the thing doesn't deserve acknowledgment or respect?

If both answers are yes, "trifling" is precisely the right word.
14967: A trigger is something that starts, causes, or sets off something else. Think of it as the first domino that makes all the other dominoes fall. The thing that makes things happen.

A trigger is the small lever on a gun that you pull with your finger to fire it. It's that curved piece of metal tucked under the barrel. Pulling it starts the whole mechanical process inside the gun that results in it shooting.

This is the oldest and most literal meaning of the word. It's a small, simple part, but it has enormous power — a tiny pull of the finger causes a massive reaction.

"He held the gun steady and slowly squeezed the trigger."
2. Extended to Other Devices and Mechanisms

Because the gun trigger works so well as a concept — a small input causing a large action — the word got applied to similar parts in other devices. Any small mechanism that activates or releases something bigger can be called a trigger.

Examples: the lever on a spray bottle that you squeeze to release the liquid, the mechanism in a camera that takes the photo when pressed, or the button-like device on a power drill. These aren't guns, but they work on the same principle: you activate something small, and a bigger action follows.
3. The Figurative Meaning — A Cause or Starting Point

This is where the word becomes truly powerful and widely used. In everyday language, a trigger is any event, action, condition, or thing that directly causes something else to happen — especially something intense, sudden, or significant.

You don't need a gun or any device at all here. A trigger in this sense is simply the thing that started it.

"Stress is a well-known trigger for headaches."

"The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand is often cited as the trigger for World War I."

"A drop in investor confidence was the trigger for the stock market crash."

Notice the pattern: the trigger itself might be relatively small, but what it causes can be enormous. This reflects the original gun image perfectly — small action, big consequence.

Key nuance: A trigger isn't the same as the underlying reason or root cause. The trigger is the immediate spark, not necessarily the deep problem. For example, a small argument might be the trigger for a couple breaking up — but the real, underlying reasons probably built up over months. The argument was just the thing that set it all off.
4. The Psychological Meaning — An Emotional Trigger

In psychology, and now in everyday conversation, a trigger refers to something that causes a sudden, strong emotional or psychological reaction in a person — often a negative one like anxiety, fear, anger, flashbacks, or distress.

This is especially common in the context of trauma. When a person has experienced something deeply painful or frightening, certain things can unexpectedly bring those feelings rushing back. Those things are called triggers.

A soldier who experienced combat might find that the sound of a car backfiring is a trigger — it causes an immediate, overwhelming stress response because it sounds like a gunshot.

A person who was in an abusive relationship might find a particular phrase or tone of voice is a trigger for their anxiety.

The trigger doesn't have to be obviously related to the trauma on the surface. It just has to be something the brain has connected to the painful experience. The brain, trying to protect the person, fires off an alarm response the moment it detects that connected thing.

This is where you get the term "trigger warning" — a heads-up given before content (a video, an article, a film) that it contains material that might trigger this kind of distressing reaction in some people.

Important distinction: In casual conversation, people sometimes use "trigger" loosely to mean anything that makes them feel annoyed or upset. But in the clinical, psychological sense, it specifically refers to something that activates a deeper, often trauma-related reaction that can feel involuntary and intense — not just ordinary discomfort.
5. The Technical Meaning — In Computing and Electronics

In technology, a trigger is a signal, event, or condition that automatically starts a process or action.

In databases, for example, a trigger is a rule you set up that says: "When this specific thing happens in the database, automatically do this other thing." For instance, when a new customer is added to a customer list, a trigger might automatically send them a welcome email. The data event starts the automated action.

In electronics, a trigger is a specific input signal that tells a device or circuit to start doing something — like telling a sensor to begin recording.

The concept is the same across all these uses: a defined input sets off a predefined process.
Putting It All Together — The Unifying Idea

No matter which context you see "trigger" used in, the meaning is always rooted in the same idea:

A trigger is the specific thing whose occurrence directly causes or activates something else — often something larger, more intense, or more complex than the trigger itself.

Whether it's a finger on a gun, a drop in oil prices starting an economic crisis, a smell bringing back a traumatic memory, or a database event launching an automated process — the word always points to the thing that made the thing happen.

"Pull the trigger" — To finally make a decision or take action, especially after hesitation. "We'd been thinking about buying a house for years. We finally pulled the trigger last month."

"Trigger warning" — A notice that content may cause distress for certain people.

"Hair-trigger" — When used as a modifier (e.g., a hair-trigger temper), it means something that activates or reacts with the smallest amount of pressure — extremely sensitive. The phrase comes from guns that are adjusted to fire with barely any pull.

"Trigger point" — A specific moment, level, or condition at which something will be set off. "The trigger point for the alarm is when the temperature exceeds 100 degrees."

To trigger something means to cause it to start or happen, especially by being the direct thing that sets it off. Think of it like a domino effect — your action is the first domino that pushes everything else over.

The word comes from the physical trigger on a gun — a small piece of metal that, when pressed, immediately sets off a much larger event (the gun fires). That image captures the verb perfectly: a small or specific action that directly sets off a bigger reaction.

"Trigger" isn't just any word for "cause." It carries a specific feeling. When something triggers a reaction, there are usually two important qualities:

1. The reaction happens automatically or very quickly. The thing that gets triggered tends to be a process that takes on a life of its own once it starts. You don't have full control over it once it's set off.

2. Something was already "loaded" or "ready" to happen. The trigger doesn't create the reaction from nothing — it unleashes something that was already waiting to be released. Like a sleeping volcano that just needed an earthquake to erupt. The potential was already there; the trigger just activated it.
The Four Main Areas Where "Trigger" Is Used

1. Physical or Mechanical Actions

This is the most literal use. A device, alarm, or system starts working because something activated it.

  • "The motion sensor triggers the security lights."
  • "Pressing the red button triggers the alarm."
  • "The high temperature triggered the fire sprinklers."

Here, the relationship is direct and immediate — cause and effect, no delay.

2. Emotional or Psychological Reactions

This is one of the most common modern uses. Something in the environment causes a strong emotional or mental reaction in a person, especially one that feels involuntary or difficult to control.

  • "The smell of fresh bread triggered warm memories of her childhood."
  • "Seeing flashing lights triggered his anxiety."
  • "That song triggers a deep sadness in me every time I hear it."

Notice here that the person doesn't choose to have that emotional reaction — it just happens. The stimulus (the smell, the lights, the song) sets something off automatically. This is why "trigger" works better than "caused" in these sentences — it captures that automatic, unstoppable quality.

In therapy and mental health, "trigger" is a formal term for something that causes a person to relive trauma or experience a strong negative emotional response.

3. Medical Reactions

Something in the body or environment sets off a medical event.

  • "Stress can trigger a migraine."
  • "Pollen triggers his allergic reaction every spring."
  • "Lack of sleep triggered an asthma attack."
  • "The drug triggered a hormonal response."

Again, the "automatic" quality is strong here. The body responds without you choosing it.

4. Events, Processes, or Chain Reactions in the World

Something starts a bigger sequence of events — social, political, economic, or otherwise.

  • "The scandal triggered a wave of protests across the country."
  • "The bank's collapse triggered a global financial crisis."
  • "His resignation triggered an urgent meeting among the board."
  • "One small mistake triggered a chain of consequences."

Here, the trigger is the starting point of something much larger and more complex that follows.
Does the Person Have to Intend It?

No. This is important. "Trigger" can describe both intentional and unintentional causes.

  • A security team intentionally triggers an alarm during a drill.
  • A loud noise unintentionally triggers someone's anxiety.

Both are correct. The word doesn't judge whether the person meant to set something off. It simply describes the fact that one thing caused another to begin.

• Cause is broad and neutral. "Trigger" is more specific — it implies something sudden, automatic, and often with an explosive or chain-reaction quality. You can say "Eating too much caused his stomachache," but that doesn't feel like a trigger. A trigger is more of a switch being flipped.
  • Start / Begin tell you something began, but not what set it off. "Trigger" names the cause specifically.
  • Prompt suggests a gentle nudge that encourages something. "Trigger" suggests something more powerful and automatic — less of a suggestion, more of an activation.
  • Spark is a close cousin and is used metaphorically in a similar way ("his words sparked outrage"), but "trigger" is more precise and is used in medical, psychological, and technical language where "spark" wouldn't fit.

[Something] triggers [a reaction / an event / a process]

  • "Caffeine triggers his insomnia."
  • "The discovery triggered a new wave of research."

[Something] triggers [something] in [someone]

  • "That film triggers strong emotions in most viewers."
  • "Criticism triggers defensiveness in him."

Be triggered by [something] (passive form)

  • "The explosion was triggered by a faulty wire."
  • "Her panic attack was triggered by the crowd."

Trigger off (phrasal verb, same meaning, slightly more emphatic)

  • "His comment triggered off a heated argument."

You will very often see "trigger" used with words like: a response, a reaction, a crisis, a warning, an alert, a memory, anxiety, depression, an attack, an alarm, a discussion, outrage, a process, a collapse. This gives you a feel for the kinds of things that get triggered — they're usually significant events, strong reactions, or automatic processes.

When you use the verb trigger, you're saying: "This specific thing acted as the switch that set something else in motion." The key ideas bundled into this one word are:

  • There is a clear and direct link between the cause and the effect.
  • The effect tends to be automatic, powerful, or hard to stop once begun.
  • The potential for the effect was often already present — the trigger just released it.
  • The cause can be intentional or accidental.

Whether you're talking about an alarm, an emotion, a disease, or a historical event — if one thing flips a switch and directly sets off another, "trigger" is your word.

Before jumping into specific meanings, here is the one idea that ties them all together:

A trill is any sound produced by a rapid, repeated back-and-forth vibration or flickering motion — creating a fast, trembling effect.

Think of a hummingbird's wings. They don't flap slowly like an eagle's — they beat so fast that you can't see individual movements. A trill is essentially the sound version of that idea: something oscillating so quickly it creates a blended, shimmering effect.

This core idea plays out in three distinct areas, each of which is a legitimate and important meaning of the word.

This is the most well-known use of the word.

In music, a trill is a rapid, continuous alternation between two neighboring notes — the written note and the note just above it — repeated over and over in very quick succession.

Imagine pressing piano keys A and B, but instead of playing them one after the other slowly, you alternate between them so fast that it becomes a shimmering, buzzing blur of sound. That blurred, vibrating effect is a trill.

Think of it this way: If a regular note is a still photograph, a trill is a video clip — it's movement built into a single moment of music.

A trill is not a random wobble. It is precise and controlled. The two notes involved are always specific — the written note and the one immediately above it on the musical scale — and the alternation is kept even and steady. The performer decides how fast, but "fast" is always the defining character.

Where you hear it:

  • Classical piano and violin music are full of trills, often used at dramatic or emotional peaks.
  • Flute players use trills to create a sparkling, airborne quality.
  • Opera singers perform vocal trills to show skill and add ornament to a melody.
  • Even jazz and blues musicians use trills on the piano and guitar.

A trill in music is considered an ornament — meaning it is a decoration added on top of the main melody to make it more expressive, elaborate, or beautiful. It is one of the oldest and most universal musical ornaments in the world.
Meaning 2: In Language and Speech Sounds (Linguistics)

In the study of language, a trill is a specific type of speech sound — a consonant — produced when part of your mouth or throat vibrates rapidly against another part, due to the airflow passing through.

The organ doing the vibrating could be:

  • The tip of your tongue (vibrating against the ridge just behind your upper teeth)
  • The back of your tongue (vibrating against the back of your throat)
  • Your lips (vibrating against each other)

The most famous example is the "rolled R" — the sound you hear in Spanish words like perro (dog) or rojo (red). When a native Spanish speaker says perro, the tip of their tongue taps and vibrates against the roof of their mouth several times in rapid succession. That vibrating, rolling sound is a trill. It is not one single tap — it is multiple rapid taps fused together by the airflow.

Other examples:

  • The rolled R used in Italian (Roma), Russian, Arabic, and many other languages is a trill.
  • Some languages use a "throat trill" — a gargling-like vibration at the back of the throat — heard in certain dialects of French, German, and Portuguese.
  • A few rare languages even use a lip trill (imagine a motorboat sound, but used as a real word consonant).

The key insight here is that a trill in speech is not something most English speakers produce naturally. English does not have trill consonants. This is why English learners of Spanish often struggle with the rolled R — it requires a new kind of mouth movement that English never trained you to make.
Meaning 3: In Nature — Birdsong and Other Sounds

A trill is also used to describe a rapid, high-pitched, vibrating sound produced by birds, insects, and sometimes other animals.

When a bird sings a trill, it means the bird is rapidly repeating a short note or group of notes so quickly that they create a continuous, fluttering, musical shiver of sound. Think of the fast, bubbling song of a sparrow or wren — that rolling cascade of rapid repeated notes is a trill.

Insects like crickets and frogs also produce trills — sounds that consist of rapid pulses blended together into one continuous, trembling tone. The effect is a kind of natural music, alive with vibration.

In this meaning, a trill is not about precision (as in music) or mechanics (as in linguistics) — it is simply the name for that particular quality of fast, rippling, natural sound.

Now that you've seen all three meanings, notice how perfectly they fit together:

AreaWhat vibratesThe result
MusicTwo notes rapidly alternatingA shimmering musical ornament
SpeechA mouth organ against another surfaceA rolled, buzzing consonant
NatureA bird's or insect's soundA fast, rippling, trembling tone

(The above is just to illustrate the pattern — the word itself carries the same spirit of rapid vibration across all three.)
How "Trill" Is Used in a Sentence (as a noun)

Here are natural example sentences covering all three meanings:

  • "The violinist played a long trill at the climax of the piece, and the audience held its breath." — musical trill
  • "The Spanish 'rr' is a trill, and it took me months of practice to produce it correctly." — linguistic trill
  • "I woke up to the trill of a songbird just outside my window." — natural sound trill
  • "Her voice rose into a beautiful trill that echoed through the concert hall." — vocal/musical trill

If you ever need to recall this word in a flash:

A trill is a rapid, controlled, back-and-forth vibration that produces a shimmering, trembling effect — in music, in speech, or in natural sounds.
